title: In the 1960s, people confided in a chatbot that understood nothing
body: ELIZA, written by Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT between 1964 and 1967, worked by spotting keywords in what you typed and turning your own sentences back into questions, in the manner of a Rogerian therapist. It had no knowledge of the world: Weizenbaum chose the therapy setting precisely to sidestep giving the program any. Yet users became emotionally attached to it, and his own secretary reportedly asked him to leave the room so she could talk to it in private. Our habit of reading understanding into a machine’s words is now called the **ELIZA effect**, and it is why today’s chatbots can feel like someone is home.

slides.heading: The trick
items: Scan the sentence for keywords, each ranked by importance
Swap ‘you’ for ‘I’ and reflect the phrase back as a question
No keyword found? Fall back to a stock response

slides.text: I had not realized ... that extremely short exposures to a relatively simple computer program could induce powerful delusional thinking in quite normal people.

slides.heading: The ELIZA effect
slides.text: The effect named after the program is our tendency to assume that software producing fluent words must understand them. It drove Weizenbaum’s later critique of artificial intelligence in his 1976 book Computer Power and Human Reason.

slides.question: Why did Weizenbaum make ELIZA play a psychotherapist?
options: A therapist can just echo your words
He was training as a therapist
It was the only script that fit
slides.explanation: He chose the Rogerian setting to sidestep giving the program a database of real-world knowledge: it could keep a conversation going by reflecting the user’s statements.
